progressionInfo.name: I-IV Progression
progressionInfo.subtitle: The warm, rocking two-chord motion between tonic and subdominant - a gentle back-and-forth that underpins gospel, folk, rock anthems, and the timeless Amen cadence.

properties.label: I (Tonic)
properties.value: Home base, stability, the point of rest and resolution

properties.label: IV (Subdominant)
properties.value: Warm departure, gentle lift away from home without dominant tension

properties.label: Relationship
properties.value: A rocking shuttle between rest and gentle motion - no leading-tone pull

properties.label: Interval
properties.value: Root movement of a perfect fourth upward (or fifth downward)

properties.label: Why It Works
properties.value: IV shares two common tones with I, creating smooth voice leading and a sense of floating rather than pulling

examples.label: Common Tone
examples.value: C is shared between both chords, anchoring the motion

chordDiagrams.title: I-IV in C Major
practiceNotes: The C to F change is one of the most common on guitar
Keep your 1st finger anchored on the 1st fret when moving to F
Practice rocking back and forth every 4 beats at 70 BPM
Listen for the warm, floating quality when moving to F

chordDiagrams.title: I-IV in G Major
practiceNotes: G to C is one of the most beginner-friendly chord changes
The ring finger can stay planted on the 3rd fret as a pivot
Try strumming 4 bars of G, then 4 bars of C, and feel the lift
Great key for campfire songs and sing-alongs

advancedApplications.title: Common Variations
advancedApplications.description: Ways to expand the I-IV framework:
items: I-IV-I-IV (steady alternating vamp, great for grooves)
IV-I (Amen cadence / plagal cadence, classic hymn ending)
I-IV with added 7ths (IMaj7-IVMaj7 for a jazz or neo-soul feel)
I5-IV5 (power chord version for rock anthems)
I-IV with bass pedal (keep the tonic root sustained throughout)

advancedApplications.title: Key Transposition
items: C Major: C - F
G Major: G - C
D Major: D - G
E Major: E - (barred A shape or open riff)
F Major: F - Bb

advancedApplications.title: Rhythm & Feel Ideas
advancedApplications.description: Two chords means the groove does the heavy lifting:
items: Slow whole-note pads for hymn-like grandeur
Percussive muted strumming for funk and R&B vamps
Arpeggiated fingerpicking for folk and singer-songwriter feel
Driving quarter-note power chords for arena-rock anthems
Syncopated offbeat stabs for reggae and ska textures

examples.title: "Born in the U.S.A." - Bruce Springsteen
examples.description: Iconic I-IV vamp in B-flat drives the entire song
examples.detail: The synth riff and driving beat lock into a two-chord shuttle that never resolves to V

examples.title: "Tulsa Time" - Eric Clapton / Don Williams
examples.description: Country-rock groove built on a I-IV shuffle in E
examples.detail: The laid-back feel comes from the gentle subdominant lift and return

examples.title: "Free Fallin'" (Intro/Verse) - Tom Petty
examples.description: Opens with a repeating I-IV vamp in F major
examples.detail: The floating, weightless quality of the verse mirrors the song's title perfectly

examples.title: The Amen Cadence (IV-I)
examples.description: The plagal cadence sung at the end of hymns worldwide
examples.detail: IV resolving to I produces a warm, restful conclusion without dominant tension

examples.title: "He's Got the Whole World" - Traditional Gospel
examples.description: Classic gospel and spiritual built on I and IV
examples.detail: Simple harmonic foundation lets the melody and message shine through

examples.title: Drone-Based Folk Music
examples.description: Celtic, Appalachian, and modal folk traditions
examples.detail: Many fiddle tunes and folk songs oscillate between I and IV over a tonic drone

practiceCategories.title: Chord Transitions
items: Alternate I-IV every 4 beats at 60 BPM in C major (C-F)
Speed up to changes every 2 beats, then every beat
Practice the F barre chord - keep 1st finger barring strings 1-2
Work on pivot fingers: keep common fingers planted during changes
Try the same exercise in G major (G-C) and D major (D-G)

practiceCategories.title: Rhythm & Groove
items: Strum whole notes (4 beats each chord) and listen to the harmonic color
Try a boom-chick pattern: bass note on 1, chord on 2-and, repeat
Practice a 16th-note funk strum with ghost strokes on the I-IV vamp
Use palm muting on power chords (C5-F5) for a rock feel
Play along with gospel or folk recordings to internalize the feel

practiceCategories.title: Creative Exploration
items: Write a simple melody that floats over a I-IV vamp
Record a loop of C-F and improvise using the C major pentatonic scale
Try playing IV-I (Amen cadence) as a song ending after any progression
Experiment with dynamics: play the IV chord softer or louder than I
Layer the I-IV vamp with different picking patterns and compare the mood

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Open Chord Shuttle in C
notatedExercises.description: Practice the fundamental I-IV change with whole-note strums in C major:
practiceNotes: Hold each chord for 4 beats (one full measure)
Focus on making the F chord ring clearly on every string
Listen for the warm lift when moving from C to F
Repeat until the transition feels effortless and automatic

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 2: Gospel Amen Cadence
notatedExercises.description: Practice the plagal cadence (IV-I) as a resolving figure in G major:
practiceNotes: Play C major (IV) for 2 beats, then resolve to G major (I) for 2 beats
Let the final G chord ring and sustain fully
Try adding the progression at the end of any song you know
Sing 'Amen' over the IV-I motion to feel the cadence

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 3: Rock Anthem Power Chord Vamp
notatedExercises.description: Driving quarter-note power chords alternating I and IV in C:
practiceNotes: Use C5 and F5 power chord shapes on the A and E strings
Strum steady quarter notes with all downstrokes
Start at 100 BPM and build up to 140 BPM
Add palm muting for a tighter, more aggressive sound

sections.title: Scale Degrees
items: I (C): 1st degree - Tonic, the home chord and point of rest
IV (F): 4th degree - Subdominant, a gentle departure from home
Root movement by perfect 4th upward (C up to F)
Unlike V, the IV chord has no leading tone pulling to I
This creates a floating, open quality rather than urgent tension

sections.title: Why IV Feels Warm, Not Tense
items: The IV chord shares two notes with the I chord (C and E in C/F major)
No tritone interval exists between I and IV (unlike V7 to I)
The motion to IV feels like rising or opening up, not creating tension
Returning to I feels like settling back, not snapping into resolution

sections.title: Common Tones (C and F major)
items: C major (C-E-G) and F major (F-A-C)
C is the common tone between both chords
E moves up to F (half step - the smoothest possible voice leading)
G moves up to A (whole step)
Two of three voices move by step, creating very smooth motion

sections.title: The Plagal Cadence (IV-I)
items: Also called the Amen cadence from its use in hymns
A softer alternative to the authentic cadence (V-I)
Does not contain the leading-tone resolution of V-I
Often used as a final tag after an authentic cadence for extra closure

journeySection.description: Now that you understand the I-IV subdominant shuttle, explore how adding more chords creates richer harmonic possibilities.
